s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp.title: The SpecTag, and how a symbol carries it
s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp.text:
A SpecTag is the text `@spec <sid>`, or `@spec none` followed by its reason. The form `@spec none` stands on a symbol only.

A symbol carries its SpecTag as a line of the comment directly above it, above its decorators where it has any. That comment is:

- in TypeScript and JavaScript, the symbol's doc comment;
- in Python, a comment line.

A symbol implementing several rules carries several SpecTags. A test carries its SpecTag in its name or in a mark on it (§s-zrsc6asgmhv8tnc).

A symbol that implements no rule says so with `@spec none`, followed by the reason it carries none. Where such a symbol stands first in a run of re-exports, with no blank line between them, it says so for the whole run.

On a symbol, only the delimiters of the comment may share a SpecTag's line, so that a scan finds a SpecTag's text in any language.

Which symbol a SpecTag stands on is found by parsing the file with tree-sitter and the grammar of the file's language. The parser is used alone, with no program and no type checker.

A description of each language names what counts in it as a declaration and as a test. TypeScript, JavaScript and Python are described.
s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp.reason:
A comment above a symbol is where an editor shows a SpecTag and where a reader of the symbol is already looking.

A scan finds a SpecTag but cannot see what it is attached to, so a SpecTag standing over nothing would pass it. The parser sees the symbol under the comment. Used alone, the parser answers the same for the same file every time. Alone, it is also cheap enough to run at every commit.

One parser with a grammar per language makes a further language a description rather than new code.
s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp.split: The SpecTag's form and where a symbol and a test carry it; how the tools find a SpecTag and the symbol under it (the scan, tree-sitter alone, a description per language).

s-zrsc6asgmhv8tnc.title: How a test declares the node it is written from
s-zrsc6asgmhv8tnc.reason:
In TypeScript and JavaScript a test's name is a string, which a SpecTag can open. A run reports that name.

A Python test is named by its function, which cannot hold a SpecTag. So a Python test's SpecTag goes into a mark. The plugin puts it where a run's report shows it.
s-zrsc6asgmhv8tnc.split: How a test declares its SpecTag in each language; what the plugin `pytest-specsheriff` does with the mark.

s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u.title: Who runs the reviewer
s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u.reason:
A runner judges the code against the nodes alone, not against what its author meant. So how it is started keeps from it everything of the session that wrote the code. Print mode and `codex exec` answer once and exit, with no session around them to carry anything over.

A CLI held to the schema of the verdict answers in a form `sheriff review` can read. An answer that contradicts itself leaves open which half the reviewer meant. Taking either half would decide for the reviewer.

A shell in between reads the arguments by its own syntax. On Windows, ending that shell at the time limit leaves the CLI it started running. A command script runs only through a shell, so the program it starts is started instead.

A list of what to strip would fall behind unseen, so the environment lists what passes. An agent sets variables of its own for the session it runs, and a new release may add more. The git hooks set git's variables to the repository. A CLI started in its empty directory would then read the repository through them.

A variable the run needs, left off the list, fails the run instead. The commit is then refused, saying why.

A run of the reviewer is paid for by the user who commits, from their own account. So it runs at the models and the efforts that user has confirmed. Those settings are kept on the user's machine rather than in the project, which every clone shares.

The git hooks read the git configuration with no agent running. The configuration outlives an update or a removal of either plugin. Its global scope serves every project of the user, so one answer on each machine holds wherever they commit.

A confirmed setting holds its value, so that a release of the SpecSheriff tools offering other defaults changes nothing a user has confirmed.

Where a setting is not confirmed, the review still runs at its default. A commit whose review cannot be held is refused (§s-nyh9yk22ba6g77q). Refusing would then hold every commit of a user nobody has asked yet, as one committing from a terminal or in CI. The default is named with every review it runs, so that nobody pays long without knowing at what.

Whether code does only what its rules say is the one judgement among the checks, so it is asked at high effort. With Codex, high was the lowest effort tried at which the reviewer refused, in every run, a change it must refuse. At lower efforts it passed that change in some runs or in all.

Nothing was measured with Claude. Its runner is asked the same effort so that the two runners judge alike.

The default of the runner `claude` is `opus`, the model Anthropic names as its default, rather than its most capable model. That model costs the user more for each review. The runner falls back to `sonnet` so that a review is held where `opus` is overloaded or not offered.

Which models Codex offers depends on how its user signs in. So the default of the runner `codex` is the one Codex chooses for that account.

Codex offers no run without tools. So its runner turns off every tool a setting reaches. For the same reason, its sandbox lets nothing be written.

A user with one agent has no other to run, so the runner follows the plugin a user has. A project wanting one reviewer for everyone names it.

The limit on a run's time is long, since it ends a run that hangs rather than hurrying one that reads a large change.
doubts: Reason: kept "An agent sets variables of its own for the session it runs, and a new release may add more." as one sentence, since splitting it would have to say whose release adds them (most likely the agent's).

Reason: the first paragraph now opens with its ground ("A runner judges the code against the nodes alone") instead of ending with it as a purpose ("so that it judges..."); the owner may prefer the original order.
s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u.split: The verdict and how `sheriff review` reads it; how a runner is started and its environment; the runner `claude`; the runner `codex`; the user's settings in the git configuration, their confirmation and defaults; the project's settings in `sheriff.config.json` (which runner, the time limit).

s-v4qus7raqnwzneb.title: How an approval is recorded
s-v4qus7raqnwzneb.reason:
One line appended per approval keeps every approval ever given. The lines two branches append merge without a conflict where git merges the approvals by union, as `sheriff init` has it do (§s-7unxytshhc4md54).

SHA-256 is a hash every language provides. The email git is configured with is the one a commit names its author by. So an approval and the commit carrying it name the same person.

The owners a node names say who reads its wording, not what the wording is. What the reindex builds is no one's wording.

A fingerprint changes with the name and value of every key in its string. A release writing the wording in another form would otherwise make a draft every node approved before it, though no wording changed.

A section's and a header's status is built (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs), so nobody approves them. No edit of the approvals passes the guard (§s-83ev4wwesbwnhnp), so a line once appended can be taken out only through git. The commands therefore refuse what no line may record.

A withdrawal takes back the node's approval, not that of one of its wordings (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq). An approval left standing for an earlier wording would let an edit restore that wording with the status `approved`. With the latest line deciding, a withdrawal cannot be undone by typing a status back.
doubts: Text: "It makes the node a draft" and reason "make a draft every node" kept as the ordinary noun, not the status value `draft`.
Text: "An owner is named by an email." now stands in a paragraph of its own; its words are unchanged.
s-v4qus7raqnwzneb.split: Recording an approval (`sheriff approve`); withdrawing one (`sheriff approve --withdraw`); the fingerprint of a wording.

s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p.title: A git hook runs the SpecSheriff tools a plugin keeps on the machine
s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p.text:
When a session starts, the plugin for Claude Code (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5) copies the SpecSheriff tools it carries into its data directory. It copies them where the copy there is of another release or missing. The data directory is `<plugins>/data/specsheriff-specsheriff-marketplace/`. `<plugins>` is `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` where it is set and `~/.claude/plugins` otherwise.

The plugin for Codex CLI (§s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4) keeps no copy. Its tools stand in its directory in Codex's cache, `<Codex home>/plugins/cache/specsheriff-marketplace/specsheriff/<version>/tools/`. `<Codex home>` is `CODEX_HOME` where it is set and `~/.codex` otherwise.

`~` is the user's home directory, on Windows their profile directory.

Each git hook `sheriff init` writes holds:

- the lookup of those tools;
- a call to the script for that hook in their `hooks/`;
- what it does where it finds none;
- the run of the project's own tools (§s-n4m5zvh96yb299p).

Where the hook finds the tools of both plugins, it takes those whose `release` file opens with the higher version, compared as semantic versions. Where the two versions are equal, it takes either.

The hook's script runs what the hook is to run (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw). It refuses where Node.js is missing or older than the tools need, naming the version they need.

Where the hook finds the tools of neither plugin, it runs the project's own tools (§s-n4m5zvh96yb299p). It then lets the commit or the push through unless one of them fails. The pre-commit and pre-push hooks then say that no check of SpecSheriff ran, because they found the SpecSheriff tools of no plugin on the machine.

The script run when a session starts names each of these hooks that holds what an earlier release of `sheriff init` wrote:

- each git hook in `.githooks/`;
- each of the agent's hooks for Codex in `.codex/hooks.json`.

For each, it says that `sheriff init` replaces it (§s-7unxytshhc4md54).
s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p.reason:
Claude Code keeps each version of a plugin in a directory of its own, which changes with every update. It keeps the plugin's data directory across updates. So the plugin keeps a copy of its release there, at a path a hook written once can name.

Codex keeps the one installed version of a plugin in its cache. It deletes the cache when the plugin is removed, while it leaves the plugin's data directory. A copy kept there would outlive the plugin. So the hook looks in the cache, which goes with the plugin.

The hook looks for the tools of both plugins because a user may move from one agent to the other. It takes the higher release because that release holds every fix of the lower.

A hook that finds no tools is most often one whose user removed the plugin. Refusing would hold every commit of that user while checking nothing, so the hook lets it through and says so. The hooks stay on so that the project's own tools keep running. So the notice recurs at every commit and push.

Where the tools are found but cannot run, the plugin is there and its user expects the checks to hold, so the script refuses.

A hook is a file of the project, which only a commit changes. So a hook written by an earlier release keeps its lookup until `sheriff init` replaces it. The session start says so, because it runs in every clone.
s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p.split: The copy of the tools the plugin for Claude Code keeps, and where the plugin for Codex CLI keeps its tools; the git hook's lookup, its choice between the plugins and what it does without tools; the session start naming hooks an earlier release wrote.

s-n4m5zvh96yb299p.title: The project's own tools in a git hook
s-n4m5zvh96yb299p.text:
Each git hook `sheriff init` writes runs the project's own tools for it after the checks of the SpecSheriff tools (§s-pcnyfp7gev7syax). They are the files directly in `.githooks/<hook>.d/` whose first line names their interpreter. They run in the byte order of their names. The hook names each other file there and does not run it.

A first line names an interpreter where it opens with `#!`, followed by a path and at most one argument. A carriage return closing the line is left out.

The hook runs the project's tools whatever the checks found. That includes the script refusing where Node.js is missing or too old. The hook runs them also where it finds no SpecSheriff tools (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p).

Each of the project's tools:

- runs from the root of the working tree, by the interpreter its first line names, in git's own environment, so it reads the working tree and git's index;
- is handed the arguments git hands the hook and a copy of the standard input git hands it.

Each of them runs, whatever the others find. The hook fails where:

- the checks refuse;
- one of the project's tools ends with an exit code other than zero;
- one of the project's tools changes the staged files or the commit's message.

The hook names each of the project's tools that makes it fail.

These files are among the repository's own tools, not the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc).
s-n4m5zvh96yb299p.reason:
A repository taking up the method has its hooks in `.githooks/`, which `core.hooksPath` names. So git runs the project's own tools nowhere else. Kept in a folder of their own, the project's tools are the project's files. `sheriff init` neither replaces them nor names them as changed by hand.

Each of them runs, so that each reports what it would report alone.

A tool is chosen by its first line rather than by the executable bit. A file committed from a system that keeps no executable bit loses that bit.

The pre-push hook's input names the refs pushed, which a tool judging a push needs as the hook does.
doubts: Text: kept the first item of the list of how each tool runs whole, since splitting it would have to choose which of the root, the interpreter or git's environment "so it reads the working tree and git's index" follows from.
Text: the hook naming "each such tool" and naming the tool that changed the staged files are now one sentence: "The hook names each of the project's tools that makes it fail."

s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5.title: The plugin for Claude Code carries everything its work needs
s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5.text:
The plugin for Claude Code, `specsheriff`, carries:

- the skills `spec`, `spec-review`, `spec-adopt`, `spec-init` and `spec-remove`;
- the SpecSheriff guidelines and their schema;
- the SpecSheriff tools.

It declares its hooks to Claude Code: the agent's hooks (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw) and the one run when a session starts (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p).

It declares each setting of the runner `claude` (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u) as one of its options. Claude Code asks the user for those options when it enables the plugin. Each option names its default and takes no default value, so that a value Claude Code holds for it is one the user gave.

In a repository holding no `sheriff.config.json` at its root, the plugin's hooks do nothing but:

- keep its copy of the tools (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p);
- write the settings the user gave as its options (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw).

The marketplace `specsheriff-marketplace` lists the plugin by the relative path of its directory. A project declares both in `.claude/settings.json`:

- the marketplace under `extraKnownMarketplaces`, its source the branch `release` of the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in, and `autoUpdate` on;
- the plugin under `enabledPlugins`.

Each machine runs the release its copy of the plugin holds until Claude Code updates it there.

The plugin's skills and the agent's hooks run `sheriff` from the SpecSheriff tools the plugin carries, as `node "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/dist/cli.js"`.

The skill `spec-init` runs `sheriff init`. It then takes up the settings of the runner `sheriff review` would take. It passes over each setting the user's git configuration holds or the user was asked for (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw). For each other setting, it:

- offers the setting to the user at its default, to confirm or replace;
- writes what the user answers.

It then marks the runner asked (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u).

`spec-remove` runs `sheriff remove` (§s-7unxytshhc4md54) and then offers to remove the plugin from the machine.

The skills set neither a model nor a reasoning effort, for themselves or for any agent they start. They work at those the user has chosen in their session.
s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5.reason:
An agent takes up a skill only where it is installed. Claude Code installs and updates a plugin from a marketplace itself. It runs the hooks a plugin declares while the plugin is enabled. So, declared in the project, the plugin is offered to the agent of every clone. Updating itself, it brings every machine the latest release.

Carrying the guidelines and the tools beside the skills, the plugin keeps everything of one release together on the machine. It keeps nothing of a release in the project but the calls to it.

A plugin installed for a user runs in every project they open. A project not taking the method is held to nothing of it.

The marketplace is read from `release`, which holds only releases, so an agent loads a release and never the work in progress on `main`. Wherever a skill or a hook names `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, Claude Code writes there the directory of the plugin's installed release. So each skill and each hook runs the tools of its own release.

A plugin is installed for its user on the machine, beyond any one project. So `spec-remove` offers its removal and leaves the choice to the user.

The user pays for their session at the model and the effort they choose in it, so the skills set neither. The reviewer runs outside the session, at the cost of the user who commits and at the settings that user confirms (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u). Claude Code asks for those settings as the plugin's options when it enables the plugin.

A default value declared for an option would be taken for a user who gave none. The hooks could not tell it from an answer. So the options declare none.

Where Claude Code enabled the plugin without asking, `spec-init` asks for the settings. It asks before the first commit of a project it sets up is reviewed, unless the user was asked before.
s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5.split: What the plugin carries and the hooks it declares; the options for the settings of the runner `claude`; the marketplace and the plugin declared in the project; what `spec-init` and `spec-remove` do; the skills setting no model and no effort.

s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4.title: The plugin for Codex CLI carries everything its work needs
s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4.text:
The plugin for Codex CLI, `specsheriff`, carries:

- the skills `spec`, `spec-review`, `spec-adopt`, `spec-init` and `spec-remove`;
- the SpecSheriff guidelines and their schema;
- the SpecSheriff tools.

It declares no hooks. The agent's hooks for Codex stand in the project (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x).

The marketplace `specsheriff-marketplace` lists the plugin by the relative path of its directory, in `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json`. That file stands beside the file listing the plugin for Claude Code (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5).

The practitioner's guide, the plugin's `README.md`, gives the commands that install the plugin on a machine:

- `codex plugin marketplace add non4me/SpecSheriff@release`;
- `codex plugin add specsheriff@specsheriff-marketplace`.

The plugin's skills run `sheriff` from the SpecSheriff tools the plugin carries, as `node <plugin>/tools/dist/cli.js`. A skill takes `<plugin>` from the path of its `SKILL.md`, `<plugin>/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md`.

The skill `spec-init` runs `sheriff init --agent codex`. It then takes up the settings of the runner `sheriff review` would take. It passes over each setting the user's git configuration holds or the user was asked for (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw). For each other setting, it:

- offers the setting to the user at its default, to confirm or replace;
- writes what the user answers.

It then marks the runner asked (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u).

`spec-remove` runs `sheriff remove` (§s-7unxytshhc4md54) and then offers to remove the plugin from the machine.

The skills set neither a model nor a reasoning effort, for themselves or for any agent they start. They work at those the user has chosen in their session.
s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4.reason:
An agent takes up a skill only where it is installed. Codex installs a plugin for the user who adds it, and none that a project declares. So each user installs the plugin, as they install Codex.

Codex reads `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` before the file listing the plugin for Claude Code, so each agent finds its own plugin.

Codex admits no plugin carrying hooks into its public directory, so the plugin carries none.

Carrying the guidelines and the tools beside the skills, the plugin keeps everything of one release together on the machine. Each agent installs and updates its own plugin. So neither plugin waits on the other. Each can also change for its agent alone.

A skill reaches the tools beside it by the path of its own file, which Codex gives it.

A plugin is installed for its user on the machine, beyond any one project. So `spec-remove` offers its removal and leaves the choice to the user.

The user pays for their session at the model and the effort they choose in it, so the skills set neither. The reviewer runs outside the session, at the cost of the user who commits and at the settings that user confirms (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u).

Codex asks nothing for a plugin it installs. The session in which a project is set up started before `sheriff init` wrote the agent's hooks for Codex into the project (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x). So no session start asked for the settings there. `spec-init` asks in its place, before the first commit is reviewed, unless the user was asked before.
s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4.split: What the plugin carries; the marketplace file and the commands that install the plugin; how the skills reach the tools; what `spec-init` and `spec-remove` do; the skills setting no model and no effort.

s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x.title: The agent's hooks for Codex CLI
s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x.reason:
Codex admits no plugin carrying hooks into its public directory, so the hooks are the project's.

Codex runs a project's hooks once its user trusts the project and each hook as it stands. A hook holding only the lookup and the call changes only where its lookup does. It is then trusted again. What the scripts do follows the release.

A hook that finds no plugin does nothing, so removing the plugin leaves no hook failing in the project.

Codex hands an edit as one patch, which may touch several files. The patch is applied whole. So the guard judges each file and refuses the patch whole.
doubts: Text: the three script names kept as one list after "a call to the plugin's script for that hook", not paired with each hook, as in the original.
s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x.split: The agent's hooks for Codex and what they hold; how `sheriff guard` judges a patch of `apply_patch`.

s-pvzms7d8kxb8dk2.title: Where the types and RuntimeChecks generated from the RecordTypes are written
s-pvzms7d8kxb8dk2.text:
`sheriff types` writes the types and RuntimeChecks it generates from the RecordTypes into the files the project's technical appendix lists for them. Where the technical appendix defines no such list, `sheriff types` writes nothing.

The list of those files is defined in the rule that describes how the system generates its types and RuntimeChecks from its RecordTypes, as the rule on data structures requires (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9). That rule stands in the section of the technical appendix that describes the technologies the whole system is built with, the stack. Each path in the list is taken from the root of the repository.

A file's extension says what is written into it:

- `.ts`, the types in TypeScript;
- `.py`, the types in Python;
- `.json`, the RuntimeChecks in JSON Schema of draft 2020-12.

Those RuntimeChecks are run by the JSON Schema validator the technical appendix names. That validator asserts `format` rather than taking it as a note.

`sheriff binding` reads a file of types as the system's code even where the glob patterns naming where that code lives do not reach it.
s-pvzms7d8kxb8dk2.reason:
Which files the generated types go to is a choice covering the whole system. Such choices are described in the stack section (§s-vj7ercem526zd6v). Defined as a list in one rule, those files are read by the tools rather than looked for in prose. The tools read the levels of the domains in the same way, from a list in the project's own guidelines.

The extension already says what a file holds. A validator taking `format` as a mere note would pass an instant that is no instant.

A project with no code yet has nowhere to write the types. Read as code, a file of types has its SpecTags read, so that each RecordType's `meta.code` names the types generated from it.
doubts: Text: "as the rule on data structures requires (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9)" kept right after the rule that describes the generation, as in the original; it may be read as requiring that rule or the list itself.
s-pvzms7d8kxb8dk2.split: Where the generated files are written and what each extension holds; the validator asserting `format`; `sheriff binding` reading a file of types as the system's code.

s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b.title: What a RecordType generates
s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b.reason:
One name in every file lets a reader follow a RecordType from its node to each copy. A fixed order makes each file come out the same at every run, which the comparison of generated copies needs. The generator writes the SpecTag itself, so that the binding of each type to its node is made anew with the type and never kept by hand.

A RecordType that refines another holds that one's fields, as the schema of the nodes says. A field keeps the name its node gives because the code uses that name as it stands.

Only a RuntimeCheck can refuse an undeclared property. A type in TypeScript or Python cannot.

A name the file already uses would break its compilation or hide what it imports.

The functional form of `TypedDict` takes any field name, a keyword of Python included. A reference written as a string may name a type written later in the file, or the type itself. Python can name the object of a field only by a type of its own.
doubts: Text: in "...given a type of its own, named by the type it stands in ..., and carries a SpecTag with the same sid" I took the subject of "carries" to be that type of its own, as skills/tools/src/types.ts:308 does (it tags that type with the RecordType's sid); the owner should confirm this reading.
s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b.split: The types and definitions generated; the refusal of a name that is not an identifier or that the file already uses.

s-nk8td3ez58gahc4.title: A RecordType its variants refine
s-nk8td3ez58gahc4.text:
A RecordType that variants refine is written as the union of its members. Its variants are RecordTypes each answering to values of its choosing fields. The choosing fields are the fields whose values choose which variant a RecordType is.

The union is written:

- in JSON Schema, as a definition holding `oneOf` the members;
- in TypeScript, as a union type;
- in Python, as `<name> = Union[...]`.

Its members are:

- each variant, referred to by the name of its type;
- where some combination of the choosing fields' values has no variant, a member for those combinations.

The member for those combinations is named by the RecordType's name followed by `Other`. It has a type and a definition of its own. The type carries a SpecTag with the RecordType's sid.

A variant holds each choosing field, required and fixed to the value it answers to. It holds its own fields:

- inside the RecordType's field of type `variant`, beside the fields that field holds;
- where the RecordType has no such field, beside the RecordType's fields.

The variant's node decides whether a property nobody declared is refused there and around it.

The member for the other combinations holds the RecordType's fields, its choosing fields required where their node says so. Its definition refuses every combination of values a variant answers to. Its type gives a choosing field:

- where one field chooses, the values no variant answers to;
- where several fields choose, all its values.

The RecordType's node decides whether a property nobody declared is refused.

A field of type `variant` is required where its object holds a field and is not declared otherwise, whether or not variants refine its RecordType.
s-nk8td3ez58gahc4.reason:
A union whose members the choosing fields tell apart is how JSON Schema, TypeScript and Python each state that a RecordType's fields depend on its values. With the choosing fields required in every variant, at most one member matches.

A value that brings no fields of its own has no variant, as the rule on variants says (§s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j). So the RecordType itself answers for it, under a name its own name gives and with its own SpecTag.

Each member follows its own node on undeclared properties, so that no node's setting overrides another's. A RuntimeCheck can refuse every combination of values a variant claims. A type can name only the values each field holds, which is exact where one field chooses.

An object with no field in it holds nothing, so the field for it is not declared.

s-4npdup7mjkva69y.title: The type each neutral type of a field gives
s-4npdup7mjkva69y.text:
Each neutral type a field may have gives what the table below says, in a file of RuntimeChecks and in a file of types.

A field of type `one of` gives the values of its own list, in its order. Where its values come from elsewhere, it gives those gathered beside it (§s-ju5vcanbjph7mgh), in this order:

- by the node each comes from, the files of the specification in the code-point order of their paths and the nodes of a file in the order they stand;
- the members of one list in their order.

| Field's type | JSON Schema | TypeScript | Python |
|---|---|---|---|
| text | `{"type": "string"}` | `string` | `str` |
| email address | `{"type": "string", "format": "email"}` | `string` | `str` |
| whole number | `{"type": "integer"}`, with its bounds | `number` | `int` |

s-4npdup7mjkva69y.reason:
JSON Schema is the standard every language has a validator for. The bounds on a number's value and on how many members a field of type `list of` holds are already named in the nodes as JSON Schema names them.

Each language's own type for a value is the one its code reads without a conversion. An instant, a date and a duration travel as text, each in the form of ISO 8601 its `format` names.

A bound is carried by the RuntimeChecks alone, which run alike in every language. A type in Python can state none.

An identifier has the type of the field that identifies the RecordType it names. That way a value moving from that field to a field referring to it keeps its type and passes the same RuntimeCheck.

The generator reads a field's values in one place, whatever their source. `sheriff validate` already compares the gathered values with their source (§s-agc6fb3vx46pc23), so the generator collects nothing again. A fixed order makes each file come out the same at every run, which the comparison of generated copies needs.
